title_content.content: Strengthening mechanisms in Fe-Al based ferritic low-density steels

paragraph_content.content: Keywords: Low-density steel Strengthening mechanisms Mössbauer spectroscopy Small angle X-Ray scattering (SAXS)

title_content.content: A B S T R A C T

paragraph_content.content: Low-density steels with di<sup>f</sup>erent aluminium contents have been investigated with an aim to examine the occurrence of di<sup>f</sup>erent strengthening mechanisms leading to its higher strength. A composition corresponding to 6.8 wt% aluminium has been studied to understand the underlying strengthening mechanisms. Di<sup>f</sup>erent factors contributing to the strengthening mechanisms have been separately analyzed. Microstructural features have been analyzed using Mössbauer spectroscopy, small angle X-ray scattering (SAXS), X-ray line pro<sup>fi</sup>le analysis and transmission electron microscopy (TEM). The enhanced yield strength of the low-density steel containing 6.8 wt % Al was attributed to the strengthening e<sup>f</sup>ects arising from the ferrite grain size, dislocations incorporated during processing, ordered phase formation and the presence of Al atoms in the solid solution. Each of these operating mechanisms was modelled by using its constitutive equation for example, grain size strengthening by classical Hall-Petch equation and the strengthening from dislocations by Taylor's equation. In addition, the formation of nano-sized ordered phase was evaluated by TEM, Mössbauer spectroscopy, SAXS and hence order strengthening was modelled by using the size and volume fraction (as determined by TEM and SAXS). Strengthening due to lattice frictional stress required for dislocation motion was also incorporated into the model.

The reduction in weight of automobile components is essential for decreasing fuel consumption and hence, the exhaust gas emissions [1]. Due to its popular choice in automotive components, the density re duction of steels by the addition of aluminium (Al) has become an attractive proposition to reduce the weight of the vehicle. Addition of aluminium up to ~10 wt% leads to the formation of ferrite (Body-Centered Cubic (BCC)) phase [2] along with the density reduction of 8% [3,4]. These steels, depending on the alloying addition, can form a single phase (ferrite) [3], dual phase (ferrite + austenite) [5] or multiphase structures (ferrite + austenite + κ-carbides) [4,6,7].

Rana et al. [3] reported the development of a single phase binary Fe-Al alloy with the density reduction up to 12.7% upon the addition of 9.7 wt% aluminium. Upon the addition of Al, a reduction in Young's modulus was also reported in Ref. [3] therefore limiting its use in automotive components. The same authors in Refs. [8,9] also stabilized a duplex microstructure (ferrite + austenite) by the addition of low amounts of manganese (Mn = 3.34 wt%) and carbon (C = 0.18 wt%), which led to the precipitation of κ-carbides. The produced lean alloyed Fe-Al-Mn-C steel did not provide much promising mechanical properties (YS = 472 MPa, UTS = 635 MPa, elongation = 19.7%) in comparison to binary Fe-Al alloys. Excessive addition of manganese (> 25 wt%) along with aluminium and carbon by several other authors [10–12] have produced a multiphase microstructure producing better mechanical properties. In such cases, the precipitation of nano-sized κ- carbides in austenite matrix was responsible for the signi<sup>fi</sup>cant im provement of mechanical properties. However, dislocation motion has been attributed to consist of planar glide in spite of low stacking fault energy, possibly due to shearing of the κ-carbides particles. Steels with Mn content greater than 20 wt% also shows the formation of deformation induced ε and ′ martensite along with deformation twinning. The prevalence of twinning or martensite formation is dependent on the stacking fault energy of the steel [13,14]. However, the addition of high amount of manganese (> 25 wt%) may lead to increased cost of steel production limiting their use in automobile parts. Low-density steels having a duplex microstructure containing ferrite and austenite has also been reported [13]. These steels contain Mn (3–6 wt%) and Al (3–6 wt%) along with C (0.1–0.4 wt%). These steels deform by strain accommodation by ferrite along with deformation induced martensite formation from austenite. The substructure after deformation consisted of planar glide in austenite along with wavy slip in ferrite.

paragraph_content.content: The binary Fe-Al based low-density steels compositions developed by Rana et al. [3] was reported to possess moderate strength and ductility combination. Thus, novel strategies are needed to improve the strength of binary Fe-Al alloy with lower cost to suit for its application in automobile bodies, which requires a comprehensive understanding of the role of aluminium in the strengthening mechanisms. This paper elucidates the study of high strength low-density steels based on the binary Fe-Al composition, which could provide the basis of alloy development in this direction. A rather <sup>fi</sup>ne-scale characterization using transmission electron microscopy (TEM), Mössbauer spectroscopy and small angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) have been carried out to examine the formation of ordered phases, while the microstructural features such as dislocation density have been analyzed using X-ray line pro<sup>fi</sup>le analysis.

paragraph_content.content: To get a better insight into the yield strength of Fe-6.8Al alloy fo the cold rolled and annealed samples, the observed yield strength was deconstructed into the contribution of di<sup>f</sup>erent strengthening me chanisms by the application of empirical formulations. The application of such a procedure in literature has been reported by Kumar et al. [40] to model the strength contribution in Al-Mg-Sc alloy, by Hajy Akbary et al. [41] in Fe-3.5Mn-2.9Si-0.3 C steel and Takaki et al. [42] for a Fe-18Ni-0.001 C steel. In the present study <sup>fi</sup>ve strengthening mechanisms from (i) dislocations, (ii) grain size, (iii) ordered phase, (iv) solid solution and (v) lattice frictional stress have been used to examine the yield strength of Fe-6.8Al low-density steel in di<sup>f</sup>erent conditions. Kumar et al. [40] also used the same strengthening mechanisms to correlate the yield strength of Al-Mg-Sc alloy to the various microstructural parameters such as grain size, dislocation density and precipitate size.

Error bars can be associated with the strengthening mechanisms of (i) grain boundary and (ii) ordered phase formation. It is due to the incorporation of errors in the determination of ferrite grain size, ordered phase size and volume fraction. For the 98%CR sample, the strengthening from (i) dislocations (generated during rolling) and (ii) grain boundaries are the two dominant mechanisms. But for the annealed samples the strengthening contribution from dislocations decreases due to the reduction in dislocation density and coarsening of ferrite grains upon recrystallization. For the sample annealed for 60 min, the contribution from (i) ordering and (ii) solid solution strengthening are the major contributing mechanisms.

It is well established that in polycrystalline materials, strengthening from (i) grain size and (ii) dislocations are the two potential strength ening mechanisms. In the present case, the presence of <sup>fi</sup>ne

ordered phase has been established by Mössbauer spectroscopy, SAXS and TEM based studies. Based on the TEM and SAXS results, the ordered phase have been described to be of nano-sized dimensions with sizes ranging between 2.5 and 3.75 nm (Fig. 4). Therefore, the strengthening from nano-sized ordered phase can also be considered to be additional strengthening mechanism operating in the present case. Strengthening from ordered phase formation can be attributed to the di<sup>f</sup>erence in separation of the partial dislocations in ordered and disordered phase. This also results in the creation of an antiphase boundary between the two partial dislocations present in the ordered phase. The antiphase boundary is bounded by two dislocations (i) leading dislocation and (ii) trailing dislocation. The leading dislocation destroys the ordered structure whereas the trailing dislocation restores the ordered arrangement. This leads to the constraint on dislocations travelling in pairs thus restricting their mobility and leading to strengthening. In summary, the splitting of dislocations into super-partial dislocation in ordered phases leads to increase in <sup>fl</sup>ow stress.
Similar strengthening due to formation of <sup>fi</sup>ne particles has also been demonstrated [10,11] in Fe-Mn-Al based low-density steels. Precipitation of nanosized cuboidal κ-carbides having

type structure have been described by Gutierrez-Urrutia et al. [10] in the Fe-30.5Mn 8.0Al-1.2 C alloy. The shearing of these carbides have been shown to form narrow channels in the austenite matrix leading to signi<sup>fi</sup>cantly improved yield strength. Formation of κ-carbides by spinodal decomposition have been shown in Fe-9Al-28Mn-1.8 C by Chang et al. [11] during quenching of the steel. These carbides provide exceptional strength
during tensile testing. However, in the present study the formation of ordered phase has been achieved without major alloying additions.

[8,9] also presents an important milestone for low alloyed low-density steels where the stabilization of duplex phase microstructure consisting of majority ferrite and minor austenite phase fraction was attained for the <sup>fi</sup>rst time by the addition of relatively very less amount of Mn and C.
The present work reports the observation of enhanced yield strength in Fe-Al based low-density steels. One of the reasons for the enhanced strength is due to the formation of nano-sized

ordered phase having DO structure, although the major contributions in the overall strength is due to dislocations and grain size. The characterization of the ordered phase was done by TEM, SAXS and Mössbauer spectroscopic studies. The yield strength of the cold rolled and annealed samples were then evaluated by the numerical formulation of the known strengthening mechanisms. Based upon experimental results and analysis the following conclusions can be drawn.

ordered phase has been observed in binary Fe-Al based low- density steels. These phases have been characterized by SAXS, Mössbauer spectroscopy and TEM which shows that size of the ordered phase to be between 2.5 3.8 nm. The size of the ordered phase is observed to be increasing with the aluminium content.

2. The tensile yield strengths of the Fe-6.8Al low-density steel samples subjected to di<sup>f</sup>erent annealing conditions were modelled with the available theoretical formulations for various strengthening mechanisms. For the cold rolled sample, strengthening contributions from (i) dislocations (generated during cold rolling) and (ii) grain size/boundaries were observed to be the dominant. For the fully recrystallised samples, the contribution to the strengthening mechanisms was in the following order: (i) grain size strengthening (dominant mechanism), followed by nearly equal contribution from (ii) dislocations and (iii) ordered

phase. The material annealed even beyond complete recrystallization underwent higher extent of ordering, and hence overall strength was due to nearly equal contributions from (i) solid solution strengthening and (ii) order strengthening.
In summary, it can be stated that the dominance and interplay of various strengthening mechanisms including order strengthening lead to the enhanced strengthening in Fe-Al alloys.
